Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Animator
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Vignette:
Valeria had always thought of herself as someone who could read a room, who could sense the mood shifting before anyone else noticed. That was part of what made her a good animator—she noticed the small things, the half-second flinch, the way light changed across a face. She had never imagined that same vigilance would become a cage. At twenty-seven, she sat in a therapist’s office for the first time, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and tried to explain what had happened two years ago, when she was still living with Marco.

The relationship had started like a storyboard she’d drawn a hundred times: charming, intense, fast. But within months, the intensity curdled. The first time he shoved her, she told herself it was an accident. The second time, she told herself she had provoked him. She had been late coming home from a freelance deadline, and he had been waiting, his jaw tight. She remembered the exact sound of his palm against her cheek, the way her head snapped sideways, and then the strange, hollow silence afterward. She had stood in the kitchen, her hand pressed to her face, and thought: *I made him do this. I should have been home on time.* That thought—that she had caused it because of the way she acted—had never really left her.

Over the next several months, the abuse escalated, but so did her belief that she was responsible. She began to monitor herself constantly: her tone of voice, her posture, the timing of her texts. She thought if she could just be better, more careful, she could keep the peace. She started canceling plans with friends because she was afraid of coming home too late. She stopped answering calls from her sister because she didn’t want to explain the bruise on her wrist. She told herself she was handling it. But inside, she felt something shifting, something she couldn’t name. She had begun to feel like a stranger to herself.

When she finally left—after he grabbed her by the hair and threw her against the bathroom door—she packed a bag in the dark and drove to her cousin’s apartment. She thought the danger was over. But the danger, she soon learned, had moved inside her. She could not shake the memory of the bathroom door cracking against her spine. She would be at her desk, animating a character’s walk cycle, and suddenly she would feel the cold tile under her cheek, smell the bleach from the cleaning spray, hear the echo of his voice. The memory was not a story she told herself; it was a sudden, vivid return. She would freeze, her hand still on the stylus, her heart pounding as if he were in the room.

She began to avoid things without quite deciding to. She stopped watching movies that showed any kind of conflict between couples. She muted certain songs that had been playing in the background during the worst moments. She started working from home almost exclusively, telling her supervisor it was easier for her creative process. But the truth was that she could not tolerate being around people who raised their voices in the office—even in playful argument. Her chest would tighten, and she would feel a desperate need to leave. She began to dread meetings. She took longer routes to avoid walking past a restaurant where Marco had once yelled at her in the parking lot. She did not tell anyone why.

The consequence of all this avoidance was a slow, quiet shrinking of her world. She had always been close with her cousin, but now she made excuses to decline invitations. She stopped going to the grocery store after six in the evening, because the dim lighting reminded her of the kitchen. Her freelance work suffered—she missed two deadlines because she had spent the day in a fog of intrusive images, replaying the moment she had apologized to him after he hit her, begging him to forgive *her*. She was ashamed of that memory more than almost any other. She had acted in ways that went against everything she believed about herself. She had always thought of herself as strong, as someone who would never tolerate being treated that way. But she had tolerated it. She had stayed. She had apologized. She had tried to be better for a man who hurt her. The shame was a weight she carried in her chest, a constant whisper that she had permanently changed for the worse, that the person she used to be was gone.

Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, she could barely bring herself to say the words out loud. She was afraid that if she did, she would confirm what she already suspected: that she was broken, that she had become someone weak and cowardly, that the damage was permanent. But she had also reached a point where she could not keep living this way. She wanted to feel like herself again, even if she was not sure that person still existed. She wanted to stop flinching at nothing. She wanted to be able to work without her own mind ambushing her. She wanted to believe, for the first time in two years, that she was not the one to blame.
